# Knitting-specific prior work {#sec-knitting}

## Computational machine knitting

The MIT and CMU groups have built much of the modern toolchain:
a compiler from high-level shapes to machine instructions
[@mccann2016compiler], automatic knitting of 3D meshes
[@narayanan2018automatic], inferring machine instructions from photos of
knitted fabric with a neural network [@kaspar2019neural], and turning
cut-and-sew garment patterns into machine-knit programs
[@kaspar2021knit]. These are about *structure* (stitches, shaping) more
than colourwork, but they establish representations (stitch grids,
instruction "programs") that a chart generator should be able to export to.

## Patterns from images and sketches

The paper *Generating knitting patterns from a sketch: a CSP approach* [@knitsketch2013] *(authors not verified)* frames turning a sketch into a
knitting pattern as a CSP, an early example of constraint solving for
knitting design. Commercial and hobby "photo to chart" tools for Fair Isle
and intarsia exist (e.g. ArtPatt), but these quantise an image rather than
generate in a style.

## Stranded colourwork, Fair Isle and jacquard

Stranded colourwork (including Fair Isle) traditionally uses two colours per
row with the unused colour carried as a float behind the work
[@wikipedia_fairisle]. Practitioner guidance limits floats to roughly five
to seven stitches before they must be caught; this is craft convention
rather than a published standard *(no academic source found)*. On a
double-bed machine such as the Passap E6000, two-colour jacquard knits the
back bed in a backing structure (birdseye, stripes, etc.), so the float
limit is replaced by back-bed choices that affect density and hand. The
HiDEF Passap work (NSN-2024 report) is the right local source for these
constraints.

We found **no peer-reviewed work on style-conditioned generation of
stranded or jacquard charts** from a historical corpus. Related public
experiments exist, e.g. Janelle Shane's neural-network "SkyKnit" knitting
patterns (2018, blog post, *unverified details*), but these generate
written instructions, not charts. This gap is a reasonable contribution
for HiDEF.

## Icelandic sources

Beyond the Sjónabók book itself [@sjonabok2009], Elsa E. Guðjónsson's
scholarship on Icelandic embroidery, including *Íslenskur útsaumur*
[@gudjonsson1985utsaumur] and the posthumous *Með verkum handanna:
Íslenskur refilsaumur fyrri alda* [@gudjonsson2016refil], documents the
refilsaumur hangings that inspire the banner idea. The Textile Research
Centre Leiden also has short online entries on refilsaumur and on
eighteenth-century Icelandic counted-thread patterns [@trc_refilsaumur].
